claims.text: The initial alloy is a cast, near-equiatomic Fe-Mn-Co-Cr-Ni multi-principal-element alloy with a single-phase FCC solid solution.
The initial cast alloy has coarse grains, sluggish diffusion kinetics, and limited ductility.
Adding 0.5–1.5 at% C or N can help produce a nanocrystalline grain size below 50 nm.
Vacuum induction melting followed by high-pressure torsion or cryogenic rolling and a short low-temperature anneal will induce nanocrystallization and phase separation.
Annealing at 400–600 °C and deforming below 0.3 Tm will activate interstitial diffusion while suppressing recrystallization and grain growth.
Rapid quenching can retain the proposed metastable FCC plus HCP structure.
Interstitial C or N creates lattice distortion and local chemical fluctuations.
Interstitial addition lowers stacking-fault energy and thereby promotes twinning and an FCC-to-HCP martensitic transformation.
Interstitial carbon can support joint twinning- and transformation-induced plasticity in a metastable FCC plus HCP alloy.
Sluggish diffusion in FCC multi-component alloys can resist recrystallization.
Interstitial atoms suppress grain growth through solute drag and grain-boundary pinning.
High configurational entropy and the absence of long-range ordering prevent brittle intermetallic formation during the proposed treatment.
The proposed treatment will produce a nanocrystalline, below-50-nm FCC plus HCP solid solution without B2, Laves, or other brittle secondary phases.
The resulting alloy will have enhanced hardness and yield strength approaching theoretical limits.
The resulting alloy will retain ductility and outperform single-phase nanocrystalline counterparts in strength-ductility synergy.
Grain refinement without interstitial addition leads to grain growth or brittle intermetallic formation during processing.
Exceeding the interstitial solubility limit destabilizes the solid solution by causing carbide or nitride precipitation.
Annealing above 0.5 Tm causes rapid grain growth beyond 50 nm and can transform HCP back to FCC.
A controlled series containing 0, 0.5, 1.0, 1.5, and 2.0 at% C, with a zero-carbon processing control, can test the proposed mechanism.

The hypothesis is falsified if all interstitial-containing samples remain above 50 nm, if additions above 0.5 at% C produce brittle secondary phases instead of FCC plus HCP, or if strength does not increase relative to the interstitial-free nanocrystalline control.
